title: Broadcasting Logic
blurb: Make shapes agree from the right edge; length-1 dimensions are the universal adapter.

cells.title: Right-align the shapes, then stretch the 1s
cells.body:
Broadcasting is two rules applied to shapes aligned from the right: two dimensions are compatible if they are equal, or if one of them is 1 (or missing). Compatible pairs produce the larger length; anything else is rejected — a (3,) against a (4,) raises, no guessing.

The reasoning habit is to write the shapes padded at the left with imaginary 1s and read them column by column. A (3, 1) column against a (1, 4) row becomes a (3, 4) grid: each axis takes the max of the two lengths. No 3×4 array is materialized at broadcast time — the element pair for each output cell is computed on the fly, which is why broadcasting is both cheap and easy to get wrong.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

col = np.arange(3).reshape(3, 1)
row = np.arange(4).reshape(1, 4)
print((col + row).shape)
print(col + row)
print((np.ones((2, 3)) + np.zeros(3)).shape)   # (3,) aligns as (1, 3)

cells.title: The length-1 axis is the universal adapter
cells.body:
Most broadcasting bugs are not about the rules — they are about which axis is length 1. x[:, None] turns a shape (n,) vector into an (n, 1) column; x[None, :] turns it into a (1, n) row. Combine one of each and every output cell gets a different mix: x[:, None] - x[None, :] is the (n, n) table of x[i] - x[j].

This 'pair every element against every element' construction is the workhorse of difference tables and outer products, and it composes: subtract a (C,) mean vector from an (R, C) matrix to shift every column at once. It replaces the double loop people write in their first numpy week — and it is the foundation for the row-wise normalization later in this notebook.

demo.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 4.0])
print(x[:, None] * x[None, :])     # (3,1) * (1,3) -> outer product table
grid = np.arange(6, dtype=float).reshape(2, 3)
print(grid - grid.mean(axis=0))    # (2,3) - (3,) shifts each column

exercise.title: Center the Columns
exercise.statement:
Each column of a lab readings matrix comes from a different instrument, and every instrument has its own bias. Before comparing columns, remove each column's mean so every column is centered on zero.

Implement center_columns(a): return a float64 array of the same shape where column j equals a[:, j] - mean(a[:, j]), computed with one broadcast subtraction — a - a.mean(axis=0) style — and rounded to 4 decimal places. No loops.
constraints: a is 2-D float64 with shape (R, C), R >= 1, C >= 1
the result has the same shape, dtype float64, values rounded to 4 decimal places
column j of the result is column j of a minus the mean of column j

examples.why: column means are 3, 6, 8; each column is shifted by its own mean
a 1x1 matrix: the single column's mean is the value itself, so the result is 0.0

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def center_columns(a):
    """Subtract each column's mean from that column.

    a is 2-D float64; result is the same shape, rounded to 4 decimals.
    """
    pass
hints: a.mean(axis=0) returns one value per column. What shape does that have, and why can it be subtracted from the (R, C) matrix without any loop?
m = a.mean(axis=0) has shape (C,), which right-aligns against (R, C) as (1, C) and stretches down every row. Wrap the subtraction in np.round(..., 4) at the end.
return np.round(a - a.mean(axis=0), 4). Keep it as one broadcast expression — that is the entire lesson.
exercise.reasoning: a.mean(axis=0) collapses the row axis and leaves one value per column — shape (C,), which is exactly what column-wise work needs: right-aligned against (R, C), it behaves like (1, C) and is stretched across every row. The subtraction therefore happens once per column recipe instead of once per loop iteration. The same one-liner generalizes: any per-column statistic (std, max, first row) can be applied with one broadcast, and swapping axis=0 for axis=1 turns the same idea on rows. The final np.round(..., 4) is what makes float outputs stable across machines — the mean introduces division, so pin the printed contract to four decimals.

exercise.title: Rate x Weight Table
exercise.statement:
Shipping costs form a table: row i is a delivery zone's rate (credits per kg) and column j is a package weight class. Cell (i, j) is the cost of shipping weight class j through zone i: rates[i] * weights[j].

Implement times_table(rates, weights): given the two 1-D int lists, return the full (len(rates), len(weights)) int64 table built with broadcasting — turn one list into a column and the other into a row, then multiply once. No loops, and avoid np.outer: it hides exactly the axis reasoning this exercise trains.
constraints: rates and weights are non-empty 1-D int lists; values may be negative or zero
the result has shape (len(rates), len(weights)) and dtype int64

examples.why: two zones against three weight classes: a 2x3 cost table
a single zone broadcast against four weights still yields a full 1x4 row

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def times_table(rates, weights):
    """Return the (R, C) table rates[i] * weights[j] via broadcasting.

    rates and weights are 1-D int lists; the result is int64.
    """
    pass
hints: You need every rate to meet every weight. If rates becomes a column (R, 1) and weights a row (1, C), what shape does their product get — and which axis came from which list?
np.asarray(rates)[:, None] gives (R, 1) so rates vary along rows; np.asarray(weights)[None, :] gives (1, C) so weights vary along columns. Their product broadcasts both to (R, C).
r = np.asarray(rates, dtype=np.int64)[:, None]; w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.int64)[None, :]; return r * w.
exercise.reasoning: Inserting a length-1 axis with None is how you choose which vector owns which output axis: rates[:, None] is (R, 1), so rates vary along axis 0; weights[None, :] is (1, C), so weights vary along axis 1. Broadcasting then stretches both to (R, C), and every cell is the product of its row label and its column label — an outer product computed without any intermediate loop. This layout decision is the transferable core: distance tables, coordinate grids and heatmaps are all 'pick which 1-D quantity is the row, which is the column, insert the axes, let the ufunc fill the grid'. np.outer does the same arithmetic but teaches nothing about axes — which is why it is discouraged here.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def times_table(rates, weights):
    """Return the (R, C) table rates[i] * weights[j] via broadcasting."""
    r = np.asarray(rates, dtype=np.int64)[:, None]
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.int64)[None, :]
    return r * w

exercise.title: Pairwise Difference Matrix
exercise.statement:
You have one reading per sensor and want to compare every sensor against every other: entry (i, j) of the report is sensor i's reading minus sensor j's reading.

Implement pairwise_deltas(x): x is 1-D float64 of length n. Return the (n, n) float64 matrix d with d[i, j] = x[i] - x[j], rounded to 4 decimal places, built from one broadcast subtraction of a column against a row — no loops.
constraints: the result has shape (n, n), dtype float64, rounded to 4 decimal places
rows are the minuend: d[i, j] = x[i] - x[j], so d[0, 1] = x[0] - x[1]

examples.why: two equal sensors: every pairwise difference is 0.0

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def pairwise_deltas(x):
    """Return the (n, n) matrix d[i, j] = x[i] - x[j], rounded to 4 dp.

    x is 1-D float64; the result is float64 of the same rounding rule.
    """
    pass
hints: You want x[i] to depend only on the row and x[j] only on the column. How do you turn one 1-D vector into a pure column and a pure row?
x[:, None] is an (n, 1) column and x[None, :] a (1, n) row; their difference broadcasts to (n, n), with the row lane supplying x[i] and the column lane supplying x[j].
x = np.asarray(x, dtype=np.float64); return np.round(x[:, None] - x[None, :], 4). The diagonal is zero by construction — a free sanity check.
exercise.reasoning: The orientation is the whole exercise: x[:, None] places x[i] along rows (it repeats across columns), x[None, :] places x[j] along columns, so the broadcast difference pairs each row value with each column value exactly once per cell. Every 'compare all against all' computation — differences, ratios, equality masks, distances — is this same two-adapter pattern; once the axes are assigned, the ufunc does n² pieces of work in one call. Two free invariants come with the construction: the diagonal is exactly zero, and the matrix is antisymmetric (d[j, i] = -d[i, j]). Invariants like these are cheap assertions that catch axis-assignment mistakes in any code that builds such tables.

exercise.title: Peak-Normalized Rows, Zero-Safe
exercise.statement:
Each row of a monitoring matrix is one sensor's trace. To compare shapes across sensors, normalize every row by its own maximum: row i becomes a[i] / max(a[i]).

Dead channels break the naive formula: a row whose maximum is 0 or negative has no positive peak, and dividing by it produces inf/nan garbage. House rule: such rows are reported as all zeros.

Implement normalize_rows(a): return a float64 array of the same shape where row i is a[i] / m[i] with m[i] = max(a[i]) if m[i] > 0, else all zeros. Round to 4 decimal places. Keep the row maxima in a trailing length-1 axis so one np.where decides per row — no loops.
constraints: a is 2-D float64, R >= 1, C >= 1; values may be negative or zero
a row is dead iff its max is <= 0; dead rows come back as all zeros
result: same shape, float64, rounded to 4 decimal places

examples.why: row 0 divides by its peak 12; the all-zero row and the all-negative row are dead and come back as zeros
two live rows: each divided by its own max, not by a global one

exercise.starter:
import numpy as np

def normalize_rows(a):
    """Divide each row by its max; rows with max <= 0 become zeros.

    a is 2-D float64; result is the same shape, rounded to 4 decimals.
    """
    pass
hints: Compute the per-row maxima first. What shape must they have so that a single np.where can make one decision per row and apply it across the whole row?
m = a.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) gives (R, 1). Build a safe divisor np.where(m > 0, m, 1.0) so the division is always finite, then np.where(m > 0, a / safe, 0.0) replaces the dead rows.
m = a.max(axis=1, keepdims=True); safe = np.where(m > 0, m, 1.0); out = np.where(m > 0, a / safe, 0.0); return np.round(out, 4).
exercise.reasoning: The bug this exercise guards against is structural: a.max(axis=1) with shape (R,) will not broadcast against (R, C) the way you intend — it right-aligns to the last axis and divides columns by row-maxima sideways. keepdims=True leaves (R, 1), which aligns correctly and lets a single np.where apply one decision per row across all its columns. The two-step divisor — replace non-positive maxima with 1.0 before dividing — keeps the arithmetic finite: no inf or nan is ever produced, and the outer np.where discards those lanes anyway. 'Compute a safe value, then choose with where' is the general recipe for every divide-by-something-that-can-vanish problem: normalizations, rates, percentages.
exercise.solution:
import numpy as np

def normalize_rows(a):
    """Divide each row by its max; rows with max <= 0 become zeros."""
    m = a.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    safe = np.where(m > 0, m, 1.0)      # keep the division finite
    out = np.where(m > 0, a / safe, 0.0)
    return np.round(out, 4)
